name: Double-Checked Locking
intent: Create a shared object lazily and safely, taking a lock only while it does not exist yet.
scenario: A service is expensive to build, so it is created the first time it is needed. Many threads ask for it at about the same moment when the program starts.
problem: With a plain check, several threads see that the object does not exist and each builds one, so there are many instances where there should be one. Putting a lock around every call fixes that, but then every call, for the rest of the program, pays for a lock it no longer needs.
solution: Check first without the lock: if the object exists, return it, which is the fast path almost every call takes. If not, take the lock and check again, because another thread may have created it while this one waited, and only then create it. The field that holds the object must be published safely (volatile or atomic, depending on the language), or another thread can see the reference before the object is fully built.
pain: Several threads each create their own instance
A lock around every call makes a hot spot out of a one-time job
Instances that should be unique are not, so their state differs
It is hard to see the race, because it happens only when threads meet at the wrong moment
benefits: After creation, calls take no lock at all
The expensive object is built only if it is needed
Threads that arrive early wait once, and later threads never wait
whenToUse: An object is costly to create and may never be needed
Many threads share it, and creation must happen once
A lock on every access would be a measurable cost, and your language has no built-in lazy tool
whenNotToUse: When the language offers a safe lazy facility, such as Lazy<T> in C#, a function-local static in C++11 or the holder idiom in Java: use it
When eager creation at start-up is cheap enough and simpler
In single-threaded code, or in JavaScript when creation is synchronous: one thread runs your code and the check cannot be interrupted. For asynchronous creation, store the promise, as the sample does
pitfalls: Without safe publication the pattern is broken: another thread can see a non-null reference to an object that is not fully constructed
In Java the field must be volatile (this works since Java 5's memory model); before that no correct volatile-based version existed
Forgetting the second check inside the lock creates the instance twice
Python: a module-level object is created once, at import, under the import lock, which is eager rather than lazy. For lazy creation use a lock, as the sample does
Hand-written versions are easy to get subtly wrong, so prefer the language's lazy tool

roles.label: Caller
roles.description: A thread that needs the shared object and calls getInstance().

roles.label: Instance field
roles.description: Holds the reference. It must be published safely so that readers never see a half-built object.

roles.label: Lock
roles.description: Makes creation happen in one thread at a time. Only taken when the field looks empty.

roles.label: Instance
roles.description: The expensive object that is created once and shared.

quiz.question: A lazy getInstance() takes a lock on every call. After start-up, profiling shows that threads queue on that lock all day, though the object is long built. What is the best change?
options: Remove the lock, since the object already exists and a lock cannot be needed any longer
Check without the lock for a fast path, and only then lock, check again and create
Create a second object, so that half of the threads use one and half use the other
Make the lock re-entrant, so that threads can take it again without waiting for each other
quiz.explanation: Double-checked locking skips the lock once the object exists and still protects creation. Removing the lock allows two threads to create the object at the start, and two objects defeat the purpose. A re-entrant lock helps only the same thread.

quiz.question: A Java team writes double-checked locking with a plain, non-volatile field. Rarely, a thread throws an error from inside the shared object, as if its fields were empty. What is the cause?
options: The reference can become visible to another thread before the object's fields do, so it must be volatile
The lock was released too early, so two threads created the object at the same moment
Java reuses objects between threads, which resets their fields without warning
The second check is missing, so a thread overwrote a fully built object with an empty one
quiz.explanation: Without safe publication, the write of the reference may be seen before the writes to the object's fields. Marking the field volatile gives the ordering guarantee. The lock itself is fine, and Java does not reset objects, and a missing second check would make two instances, not an empty one.

quiz.question: A C# team wants a service that is created on first use and shared by many threads. They plan to hand-write double-checked locking. What is the best advice?
options: Write it by hand with a lock, because the built-in tools are too slow for shared services
Create it in a static constructor and never use Lazy<T>, whatever the service needs
Use a plain check without any lock, since .NET objects are always built before their reference is stored
Use Lazy<T>, which is thread-safe by default, instead of writing the double check yourself
quiz.explanation: The language already offers a tested lazy, thread-safe wrapper, so hand-written versions only add the risk of subtle mistakes. A static constructor is thread-safe and runs when the type is first used, but you cannot control exactly when it runs, and Lazy<T> says what you mean. A check without any lock allows two instances.
